rv.q: The jokes are plentiful and well executed enough that if you don’t like one bit of wordplay or slapstick or song, there’s a fair chance you will like the next.
It’s fun enough, but you may want to save your shekels.

New role: Griff Rhys Jones as Harpagnon in The Miser which is showing at the Garrick Theatre The Miser tells of Harpagon, a tight-fisted Parisian who decides he will marry his son Cleante’s girlfriend, Marianne (Ellie White, rather good). His daughter Elise, meanwhile, has fallen for manservant Valere.

It also has two big assets in Griff Rhys Jones, returning to the stage after a seven-year gap, and Lee Mack, who, astonishingly, is making his straight-play debut. But the production’s anything-for-a-laugh approach means we miss the point that this play, like all great comedies, has a tragic undertow.
Now in his sixties (the same age as Harpagon) he has lost none of his energy and his comic timing is perfect.

Not that anyone would know it from seeing Sean Foley’s current production, which makes TV’s ’Allo ’Allo look like Chekhov. Foley, who also adapts along with Phil Porter, displays so little faith in the play that he fills it with lame gags, tedious audience participation and groan-inducing contemporary references.

Every now and then a show which deserves to be left at the interval – especially given today's prices – comes along and this is such a show, a dazzling addition to the list of unforgettable productions to disgrace the West End.
